title: CHAPTER ELEVEN. The same is demonstrated certainly future from the New Testament
english: CHAPTER ELEVEN. That the same is certainly future is demonstrated from the New Testament.

We have seen that in the Old Testament the resurrection of the flesh as certainly future is clearly enough foreshadowed, preached, and promised: now we shall see it taught in the New Testament so clearly as if written by a sunbeam.

title: II–III. Partly asserted, partly proved; asserted by divine authority
english: II. And there it is partly asserted, partly proved.

III. It is asserted by testimonies of divine authority. The bare assertion of it in the NT suffices for all Christians, because its authority is divine and deservedly received by Christians. It is plainly brought forward at John 5:28; 6:39–40; 11:24; Luke 24:14; Acts 17:18 and 23:6 and 24:15; Phil. 3:21; 1 Thess. 4:14; 1 Tim. 4.

title: IV. Proved by solid reasons — Ratio I from Christ's resurrection and our union with him
english: IV. It is proved by most solid reasons. Although the bare Apostolic assertion of this dogma suffices, yet lest anything be lacking against deniers and sophists, it is also proved through the whole of 1 Cor. 15.

Ratio I. From Christ's resurrection and our conformity and conjunction with Christ as members with the head, v.13: If there is no resurrection of the dead, Christ also has not been raised. The consequence is proved: (1) if there is utterly no resurrection, neither did Christ rise, since he was one of the dead; (2) he called himself the vine and us the branches (John 15:5) and is head of the body, the Church (Col. 1) — so if the joined members remain dead, the head itself also remains in death. From the same principle Paul argues at 1 Thess. 4:14. Then, the consequent granted, many absurdities follow: vain preaching; vain faith; we still in our sins; the Apostles false witnesses of God; those who fell asleep in Christ have perished.

title: Ratio II from providence; Ratio III baptism for the dead — early interpretations
english: II. From God's providence, by which it must finally go wellof whom in this life it goes ill, v.19. And v.20 he returns to the first reason.

III. From baptism for the dead, v.29. This reason is difficult and has strangely exercised the most learned interpreters. First Epiphanius (Haer. 28 on the Cerinthians) reports some who, when someone died without baptism, substituted another to be baptized for the dead. Second, others of those baptized when near death — preferred by Calvin, Vermigli, Gualther, Hemmingsen. Third Chrysostom on Marcionite abuse; he expounds of confession of the resurrection before baptism. Fourth Sedulius and the schoolmen of the death of sin. Fifth Bellarmine of the baptism of tears for purgatory. Sixth Guilandus and the Leiden theologians of martyrdom. Seventh Major of baptism over graves — of which custom there is no trace. Eighth of sepulchral washing. Ninth Camerarius. Tenth Scaliger of annual refrigerium.

title: Baptism for the dead: preferred ad hominem reading; Corinthian abuses
english: Of all opinions that seems truest which is most ancient — and what some have gathered from Tertullian by presumption should be admitted — and thence the Apostle after his manner argues ad hominem: which is also Musculus's judgment. For the simple and customary acceptation of the words is preserved. Further it is certain the Corinthian church was not very pure then, and as Scaliger notes, deadly rites and errors had then begun. So it is no wonder men so stained with errors erred about baptism's administration.

If it be objected that the Apostle nowhere rebukes this abuse: Answer with Chrysostom — one need not answer to farces. The article shows not all but some were baptized for some; he notes only those who did this, and of them shortly after said v.34: Awake to righteousness and sin not.

title: Ratio IV from hope of sufferers; Cap. 11 close before Cap. 12
english: IV. From the hope which the Apostle connects with the foregoing; opposing to the opinion of those who act wrongly the sure hope of those who suffer gloriously, and confirming the resurrection from this also as from that, vv.30–32: unless there is a resurrection of the dead and hope of recompense, he and all who undergo extremities for truth and Christ will have been in vain. Why, he says, are we in danger every hour? If after the manner of men — for praise or gain or some other cause for which secular men face dangers — I fought with beasts at Ephesus (against wicked men such as Demetrius, Acts 19), what does it profit me? Finally, if the dead are not raised, we shall not only in vain expose our heads to so many dangers, but rather will join those who say: Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die.
